questions.question:
int x=126,y=105;
 do {
	 if(x>y) x=x-y; 
	else y=y-x; 
      } while(x!=y); 

printf("%d",x);
The output of the given C code segment is ________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
This loop is exactly the subtraction-based Euclidean algorithm for computing [latex]\gcd(x,y)[/latex], repeatedly subtracting the smaller from the larger until they're equal (which happens exactly at their GCD).

[latex]\gcd(126,105)[/latex]: [latex]126-105=21[/latex]; then [latex]105-21=84[/latex]; [latex]84-21=63[/latex]; [latex]63-21=42[/latex]; [latex]42-21=21[/latex] — now [latex]x=y=21[/latex], loop ends.

Answer: 21

questions.question:
In a binary tree with n nodes, every node has an odd number of descendants.
Every node is considered to be its own descendant. What is the number of nodes
in the tree that have exactly one child?
questions.explanation:
If a node had exactly one child, its descendants = itself + child's descendants = 1 + odd = even, which contradicts the condition.

So no node has exactly one child.

Answer: 0

questions.question: Suppose a binary search tree with 1000 distinct elements is also a complete binary tree. The tree is stored using the array representation of binary heap trees. Assuming that the array indices start with 0, the 3rd largest element of the tree is stored at index _______.
questions.explanation:
Complete tree with 1000 nodes (indices 0-999). Children of i: [latex]2i+1[/latex], [latex]2i+2[/latex].

- Largest = go right as far as possible: 0 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 14 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 30 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 62 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 126 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 254 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 510. Its children 1021, 1022 do not exist, so index 510 is the largest.
- 2nd largest = predecessor of 510. It has no left child, so it is its parent: index 254.
- 3rd largest = maximum of the left subtree of 254. Left child = 509; its children 1019, 1020 do not exist, so it is 509.

Answer: 509

questions.question:
Consider a sequence [latex]a[/latex] of elements [latex]a_0 = 1, a_1 = 5, a_2 = 7, a_3 = 8, a_4 = 9, \; and \; a_5 = 2[/latex]. The following operations are performed on a stack [latex]S[/latex] and a queue [latex]Q[/latex], both of which are initially empty.

I: push the elements of a from [latex]a_0[/latex] to [latex]a_5[/latex] in that order into [latex]S[/latex].
II: enqueue the elements of a from [latex]a_0[/latex] to [latex]a_5[/latex] in that order into [latex]Q[/latex].
III: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
IV: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex].
V: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
VI: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex].
VII: dequeue an element from [latex]Q[/latex] and push the same element into [latex]S[/latex].
VIII: Repeat operation VII three times.
IX: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].
X: pop an element from [latex]S[/latex].

The top element of [latex]S[/latex] after executing the above operations is ___.
questions.explanation:
After I and II: S = [1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2] (top = 2), Q = [1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2] (front = 1).
- III: pop S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 2
- IV: dequeue Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 1
- V: pop S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S = [1, 5, 7, 8]
- VI: dequeue Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] removes 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q = [7, 8, 9, 2]
- VII + VIII (4 times): move 7, 8, 9, 2 from Q to S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S = [1, 5, 7, 8, 7, 8, 9, 2]
- IX, X: pop 2 and 9 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] top = 8

Answer: 8

[latex]{*}\text{ptr}=c[/latex] → sets [latex]a=20[/latex] (since ptr points to [latex]a[/latex], and we assign it [latex]c[/latex]'s current value [latex]20[/latex]).

[latex]c={*}\text{ptr}-a[/latex] → [latex]{*}\text{ptr}[/latex] is [latex]c[/latex] itself (since ptr points to [latex]c[/latex]), whose value is still [latex]20[/latex] (unchanged since it was first set); so [latex]c=20-a=20-11=9[/latex].

questions.question:
An array [latex]A [/latex] of length [latex]n [/latex] with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index [latex]1 \leq i \leq n [/latex] such that [latex]A[1..i] [/latex] is sorted in the non-decreasing order and [latex]A[i+1..n] [/latex] is sorted in the non-increasing order.
Which ONE of the following represents the best possible asymptotic bound for the worst-case number of comparisons by an algorithm that searches for an element in a bitonic array [latex]A [/latex]?
questions.explanation:
A bitonic array first increases then decreases (or vice versa). At any index, comparing the current element to its neighbors tells you which "half" (increasing or decreasing) you're in, and binary search can be adapted to search each half:

First locate the peak (maximum) element using a binary-search-style approach in [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex] (comparing an element to its neighbors to decide which direction has the larger values). Once the peak is found, the array splits into two ordinary sorted sequences (one increasing, one decreasing), and each can be searched with ordinary binary search, also [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex].

Combining these steps keeps the total worst-case comparisons at [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex], matching what you'd get for a single sorted array — no better bound like [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex] is achievable (you must still narrow down the location), and no worse bound like [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] or [latex]\Theta(\log^2n)[/latex] is necessary.

Answer: Θ(log n)

Click here for detail solution
